nameStory: The satiny willow gets its lovely name from the silky, lustrous sheen on the undersides of its leaves, which shimmer like fine satin fabric when caught in the light. When a breeze flips the leaves, the whole shrub seems to glow with a silvery-white radiance. The scientific name 'pellita' means 'covered with skin' or 'hide-like,' referring to the dense, felt-like hairs that create this satiny appearance.
description: Satiny willow is a medium-sized shrub that typically grows 6-12 feet tall in wetland areas across northern New England. It has narrow, lance-shaped leaves that are green on top but covered with dense, silky white hairs underneath, giving them their characteristic satiny sheen. Like other willows, it produces fuzzy catkins (flower clusters) in early spring before the leaves fully emerge. This attractive native shrub is perfectly adapted to life in boggy, acidic soils where many other plants struggle to survive.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves 2-4 inches long with distinctive silvery-white undersides covered in dense, silky hairs that feel soft to the touch. The contrast between the dark green top and satiny white bottom is striking when leaves flutter in the breeze.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, fuzzy catkins appear in early spring on bare branches. Male catkins are yellowish and about 1 inch long, while female catkins are slightly longer and greenish-white. They have a subtle, sweet fragrance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a rounded, multi-stemmed shrub 6-12 feet tall with flexible, reddish-brown to gray branches. Young twigs often have a purplish tint and feel smooth when you run your fingers along them.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth, gray-brown bark on older stems with shallow furrows. Young branches are often reddish-brown and have a slightly waxy feel when touched.

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Small, pointed buds pressed close to the stem, covered in fine hairs and often reddish-brown in color. Winter buds are tiny but noticeable against the smooth bark.

habitat: Satiny willow thrives in acidic wetlands, bogs, and swamps throughout northern New England, particularly in Vermont, New Hampshire, and Maine. It grows best in consistently moist to wet, peaty soils and is often found alongside other bog plants like leatherleaf, bog rosemary, and sphagnum moss. You'll typically spot it around the edges of beaver ponds, in wet meadows, or in boggy depressions where the soil stays saturated most of the year.

seasonality.spring: Fuzzy catkins emerge before the leaves in March-April, creating a soft, textured appearance. New leaves unfurl showing their bright green tops and silvery-white undersides most dramatically.
seasonality.summer: Full foliage displays the characteristic satiny leaf undersides beautifully. The shrub forms a dense, rounded crown with leaves that shimmer silver-white when moved by wind.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn pale yellow before dropping, and the silvery undersides become even more pronounced. Small, capsule-like fruits split open to release tiny seeds with white, cottony fluff.
seasonality.winter: Bare reddish-brown branches show the smooth bark and small, pointed buds. The multi-stemmed growth pattern and wetland location help with identification when leaves are absent.

funFact: The silky hairs on satiny willow leaves aren't just for show—they actually act like tiny mirrors, reflecting excess sunlight and helping the plant stay cool in the intense summer sun that beats down on open wetlands, while also reducing water loss in these surprisingly harsh bog environments.
confusionNotes: Satiny willow is most easily confused with silky willow, but satiny willow has much denser, more luxurious white hairs underneath its leaves that create a true satiny sheen, while silky willow's leaf undersides are more grayish and less dramatically contrasted. Memory trick: 'Satiny shimmers, silky's subtler.'
compareHints: Among New England's many willows, satiny willow stands out for having the most dramatically silvery leaf undersides—much more pronounced than the similar silky willow or sage-leaf willow. Unlike pussy willow which is famous for its large, fluffy catkins, satiny willow's catkins are smaller and less showy. It's also more consistently shrub-sized compared to black willow or white willow which can become large trees.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's many willow species, pussy willow stands out for its exceptionally soft, silvery catkins that appear before the leaves.
Bearberry willow is instantly distinguished from all other New England willows by its unique prostrate growth - every other willow species grows upright as shrubs or trees.
Among New England's willows, heart-leaved willow stands out for its combination of thick, persistently fuzzy-bottomed leaves with heart-shaped bases.
Among New England's willows, Bebb's willow stands out for its dense thicket-forming habit and adaptability to various soil types.

Among New England willows, rusty willow is most similar to grey willow (Salix cinerea), but rusty willow's twigs have that distinctive reddish-brown coloration versus grey willow's more grayish twigs.
Among New England's many willow species, black willow stands out as the largest tree form with the darkest bark.
Among New England willows, prairie willow is unique in preferring dry, sunny sites while most others need moist to wet conditions.
Grey willow differs from native pussy willow by having much more pronounced silvery-gray, woolly leaf undersides and tends to form denser thickets.
Among New England's many willows, silky willow stands out for its distinctly silky leaf undersides - most other willows have smooth or only lightly hairy leaf backs.
Interior sandbar willow stands out from other New England willows by having the narrowest leaves in the genus - much thinner than pussy willow's oval leaves or black willow's lance-shaped ones.
Meadow willow is much shorter and more colony-forming than most other New England willows like black willow or pussy willow.
Among New England's willows, shining willow stands out for its exceptional height and mirror-like leaves.
Among New England's willows, purple willow is unique for its purple-red bark and blue-green leaves - pussy willow has gray bark and broader leaves, while black willow has dark, furrowed bark.

Unlike the familiar pussy willow with its large, fuzzy catkins and broad leaves, or the water-loving black willow with its narrow leaves, tea-leafed willow has those distinctive thick, oval leaves with prominent parallel veining.
Among New England willows, sage-leaf willow is unique for its distinctly fuzzy, silvery leaves that truly resemble herb sage.
Among New England's many willows, balsam willow is unique for its strong balsam fragrance - most other willows are essentially scentless.
Among New England willows, least willow is unmistakable due to its ground-hugging growth - all other willows in our region grow as upright shrubs or trees.
Bog willow differs from its willow relatives by staying much shorter and preferring acidic bog conditions rather than streamside locations.
Among New England's willows, white willow stands out for its especially silvery leaf undersides and larger mature size.
Unlike the familiar pussy willow with its large, showy catkins and bigger leaves, or the tall black willow found along rivers, Labrador willow stays remarkably small and compact.
Unlike native New England willows such as pussy willow or black willow, dappled willow has variegated foliage and often opposite leaves rather than alternate ones.

Among New England willows, autumn willow stands out for its completely hairless leaves and stems - unlike pussy willow's fuzzy twigs, silky willow's silky leaf undersides, or meadow willow's slightly hairy stems.
Among New England's willows, blueleaf willow is distinguished by its blue-green foliage color - most other willows have bright green or silvery leaves.
Unlike other New England willows such as pussy willow or black willow that have upright or spreading branches, weeping willow is unmistakable due to its pendulous, drooping branch structure.
Among New England's willows, peachleaf willow stands out for its impressive tree size - most of our native willows like pussy willow or silky willow are shrubs or small trees.
Unlike most New England willows which have narrow, lance-shaped leaves, goat willow stands out with its broad, oval, wrinkled leaves that look more like those of a poplar or apple tree.

Basket willow stands out among New England's willows for its extremely narrow leaves and exceptionally long, straight, flexible branches - most native willows like pussy willow or black willow have broader leaves and shorter, less flexible shoots.
Among New England's many willow species, rose-gold pussy willow stands out for its ornamental catkin colors - most native willows like common pussy willow have plain silver-gray catkins.
